Question: What is your favorite derivation of Lorentz transformation?
Answer: I’ll have a crack at this question, tackling it using some very intuitive physical steps. I’ve read the derivation by Einstein and recall my first relativity lectures mentioning rulers and clocks and my eyes glazed over and it never really stuck. So I went searching for a more intuitive route. The two postulates of special relativity are the relativity postulate; that there is no privileged reference frame, and that all observers measure the same speed of light. The relativity postulate was first proposed by Galileo. Most simply put, it just boils down to vectorial addition of velocities. In one dimension, consider two coordinate systems, one stationary and one moving at some velocity, V . The velocity of an object moving with velocity v , in the stationary frame is observed to move with velocity v ′ in the moving frame. The two observations can be compared by adding the coordinate frame velocity, V such that v = v ′ + V This is just a velocity addition formula. Nothing surprising so far. We can write this in terms of position and time as follows, d x d t = d x ′ d t + V Integrating both sides with respect to t , gives, x = x ′ + V t where we have chosen the initial coordinate values to be zero. It’s actually convention to rearrange the above transformation so that the moving coordinates are defined in terms of the stationary reference, giving the standard form for the Galilean transformation, x ′ = x − V t also we have assumed a global time, t ′ = t Nothing too hard thus far. We have just shown that velocity addition implies the Galilean relativity transformation. Now on to special relativity… Let’s add a constraint that all observers in relative motion measure the same vacuum speed of light, c . That means that all observers agree that, d x d t = ± c or, d x = ± c d t There are actually two equations satisfying the condition, corresponding to light travelling in opposite directions. That’s because velocity is a vector and we must take into account the direction of travel. However, there is a convenient way to reduce the two equations into just a single constraint, and that is by squaring both sides. Thus we have the constraint that all observers must agree with, d x 2 = c 2 d t 2 or simply, d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 = 0 We can easily generalise this to three dimensions, but for brevity we’ll continue with just one dimension. As all observers in relative motion must agree with the above expression, we can equate the measurements made in different frames of reference, d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 = d x ′ 2 − c 2 d t ′ 2 Already we start to see something interesting. In general, d x ′ ≠ d x , so we must have d t ′ ≠ d t . This is a departure from the Galilean relativity, where time was considered absolute. In order for all observers to measure the same vacuum speed of light, time must be relative as well as distance. We will use the above equation to derive the Lorentz transformations. The first point to note is that whatever form the final transformation should take, it must reduce to the Galilean transformation in the low velocity limit. Thus we start with the Galilean transformation for position and insert in into the equation above to get, d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 = d x 2 − 2 V d x d t + V 2 d t 2 − c 2 d t ′ 2 This constrains the form of the time transformation because we must generate another − 2 V d x d t cross term in order for it to cancel. Thus the time transformation must have the form, d t ′ = d t − V d x c 2 This will eliminate the cross term leaving, d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 = d x 2 + V 2 d t 2 − c 2 d t 2 − V 2 c 2 d x 2 collecting like-terms on the right, d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 = ( 1 − V 2 c 2 ) ( d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 ) Note however that the above expression is not an equality. To rectify this we need to remove the factor of ( 1 − V 2 c 2 ) , which is readily accomplished by multiplying each of the transforms by the inverse square root of this factor. Thus we have the Lorentz transformations below, x ′ = γ ( x − V t ) t ′ = γ ( t − V x c 2 ) where, γ = 1 √ 1 − V 2 c 2 This is the most direct route to the Lorentz transformations that I have found that clearly shows how they are a consequence of all observers agreeing on measurements of the speed of light. Furthermore, we can take things a little bit further. Consider once more the agreement between observers regarding the speed of light, d x 2 − c 2 d t 2 = d x ′ 2 − c 2 d t ′ 2 This equation is actually more general in that it equates measurements made in two coordinate systems. Consider a stationary system, where d x = 0. Then we have, c 2 d t 2 = c 2 d t ′ 2 − d x ′ 2 The stationary frame cannot refer to light, but to some general rest frame. This tells us that there is a quantity, c 2 d t 2 that all observers agree on. We call this proper time, τ . Then we can write, c 2 d τ 2 = c 2 d t 2 − d x 2 This is the invariant spacetime interval. The expression for proper time is always positive and greater than zero. This defines a set of inertial reference frames containing a rest frame that can never reach the speed of light (because c 2 d τ 2 is always greater than zero). The interval of proper time is used to categorise separated events according to the following criteria: d τ 2 > 0 … Time-like d τ 2 = 0 … Light-like d τ 2 < 0 … Space-like Time-like events are causally connected. Light-like events define the boundary of causally connected events. Space-like events are not causally connected (which means that different observers can disagree on the causal ordering of events). Overall, the rather simple expression for the invariant proper time interval contains all of the spacetime properties of special relativity in a single compact form.

Question: If it's impossible to know the location and path of a particle at the same time, how can we see its trajectory in a cloud chamber?
Answer: That's because the cloud chamber doesn't show a precise trajectory. A classical trajectory is precise, corresponding to a unique curve. It is this uniqueness that is important. Cloud chamber tracks may resemble a classical trajectory, but they do not correspond to a unique trajectory. Rather, there are many possible trajectories that could satisfy the observed tracks. That's because the tracks have an associated volume in space. This volume is compatible with the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Cloud chamber tracks act as a sort of continuous measurement, wherein the charged particles successively interact with the medium causing the nucleation of vapour droplets. This means there is very little free evolution of the quantum wavefunction before the next measurement. This is a form of the quantum Zeno effect, where successive measurements inhibit the evolution of the wavefunction. Therefore, what you get are trajectories that look classical, but are still compatible with the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. That means the uncertainty in the position and momentum measurements are greater than or equal to one half hbar. In practice, the uncertainties are much larger than this limit.

Question: Are photons massless? Do photons have momentum? Is this momentum zero according to Einstein?
Answer: A photon is a quantum of energy in an electromagnetic field mode. If you don't understand that statement, then you probably don't understand what a photon is. That's understandable, because the quantum theory of light is not even taught at undergraduate level in most universities. So forget about photons and ask about light. Does light have momentum? Yes. This is well known and originally formulated in classical electromagnetic theory as the Poynting vector (remember momentum is a vector). Is this momentum zero according to Einstein? No. In deriving the mass-energy equivalence relationship the rather simple relationship between the energy and momentum is found, E 2 = → p 2 c 2 , or more simply, E = p c , where p represents the magnitude of the momentum. So then, are photons massless? Yes. That's because light is defined as having zero rest mass. That simply means that light can never be at rest. It must always move at the invariant velocity, c according to all observers. This property of light makes it different from any form of matter, so the Newtonian definition of momentum does not apply to light, and by extension, to photons. However, the concept of momentum transcends Newtonian mechanics. Momentum is a fundamental property that must be conserved in all physical systems with spatial translation symmetry according to Noether's theorem. Similarly, energy is a fundamental property that must be conserved in all physical systems with time translation symmetry. That means you can identify both energy and momentum in any physical system with those symmetry properties. In other words, p = m v is only applicable to particles with a non-zero rest mass. It is not the general formula for momentum. However, it is connected to light through the relativistic correction, p = γ m v . This leads to the formula for light when the rest mass is zero.

Question: What is the difference between two identical twins in twin paradox or relativity?
Answer: Two identical twins go on two different journeys. Their local clocks act as space-time odometers, keeping track of their respective journeys through space-time. If they synchronize their clocks at the beginning of their respective journeys, then if they eventually meet again, their clocks will reveal the magnitude of the difference. That's all there is to it. What most people are confused by is the symmetry of the Lorentz transformations. They conflate the transformation symmetry between two inertial frames with the entire journey from the relative perspectives of the twins. This is where the conceptual problems arise. If we consider the symmetry of the Lorentz transformations between two inertial frames of reference, then we can never realise the twin paradox. That's because the twins only meet once, so can never compare journey times. That's because Minkowski space-time is flat, so two different world lines can only intersect once. In order for the twins to meet twice, we need to consider more than two inertial frames of reference. This breaks the symmetry of the situation. Remember, the symmetry of the Lorentz transformations is only between two inertial frames of reference. A round trip (or return journey) is more complicated and needs to be treated differently. The twin paradox is taught in classes on special relativity to highlight how one needs to analyse certain problems. The students need to understand that the symmetry of the Lorentz transformations only pertains to two inertial frames of reference, not to the twins themselves.

Question: Are relativistic effects relevant in quantum computing?
Answer: In general, no. Quantum computing is based on quantum logic gates. Quantum logic gates are nondissipative and hence reversible logic gates. So what we're dealing with are gates that essentially deterministically react to some input state. As long as you have characterised the gate operation, you can write a logic table for the gate. The difference between quantum and classical logic is that quantum logic allows for superpositions of the input and output states, while there are no superpositions in classical logic gate operation. Therefore, the operation of quantum logic circuits depends on how well the physical system has been characterised. This is all done well before work commences on actually building a quantum computer. Under most circumstances, any relativistic effects are buried in the physical operation of the quantum logic gate. One possible caveat is that there may be some minor effect due to gravitational time dilation that could cause some decoherence. This effect would likely be very small (and most likely negligible), but as quantum computers become larger, it might become a source of error. However, I expect this would be one of the least significant causes of decoherence errors.

Question: Do photons in a laser beam stick together so well because they are attracted to each other gravitationally and electromagnetically?
Answer: No. Photons do not stick together. Furthermore, the photon picture of a laser beam is not trivial for a number of reasons. Bringing things down to brass tacks, photons are bosons and so satisfy Bose-Einstein statistics. What does that mean? It means that there is no limit (theoretically) to the number of photons that can occupy a field mode. What is a field mode? A field mode is a volume in space defined by certain boundary conditions. For example, the box shape of a microwave oven defines the field modes inside the oven. Those fixed modes mean that there will be both nodes and antinodes inside the oven, which will result in hot and cold spots. That's why a rotating table is added to the inside of the oven to provide more uniform heating. For a laser, the field modes are defined by the mirrors. This is called the laser cavity. The beam exits one of the mirrors, which is purposely leaky. So a laser beam can be considered a field mode. Inside the laser there is a so-called gain medium. That simply means that the medium is designed such that it will deliver more photons to the field mode than it will absorb. This is not so trivial, as a general principle is that the emission and absorption probabilities are the same. Therefore you need a special type of atom to work as a gain medium. The principle is that you need to create a population inversion. Yes, that's essentially an atom’s version of standing on your head. When you do that, there are more atoms that can emit than absorb, so photons get added to the field mode. This increases the field inside the laser cavity, and because it is a leaky cavity, a laser beam escapes to the outside. Finally, back to the boson nature of photons. Normally excited atoms can emit their photons in any direction. However, when you define a specific mode using cavity mirrors, that mode will have a slightly higher probability of capturing a photon. This is where the Bose-Einstein statistics takes over. With an increasing number of photons in the cavity mode, they act to preferentially stimulate the excited atoms to emit into the same mode. This is called stimulated emission. What ends up occurring is, light amplification via the stimulated emission of radiation (LASER).

Question: If a measurement is made on an entangled particle, and the measurement is detected on its partner by monitoring its decoherence, might that be considered instant communication of one bit of information between experimenters?
Answer: This is covered formally in the no communication theorem. Simply put, the measurement outcomes of an entangled partner appear random. Correlations only become apparent when the outcomes of both partners are compared. That means if you're off measuring one of the partners, you just receive a random bit stream (you need to measure many identical copies to build sufficient statistics). There's no way to tell if that partner is entangled or decohered. It just a random bit stream, so could correspond to either case. You can only discriminate between the entangled and decohered case by comparing your measurements with measurements made on the other particle. If they exhibit a correlation, they were entangled particles. If not, it may indicate some form of decoherence. The bottom line is that the measurement of one of an entangled particle pair delivers a purely random result from which no signal can be extracted (as per the no communication theorem).

Question: Can you provide a simple explanation of the EPR paradox for someone with no knowledge of physics?
Answer: Quantum theory has it inbuilt that you cannot simultaneously know both the precise position and momentum of a particle. This is known as the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. The EPR paradox provides an example where you could violate the Heisenberg uncertainty principle with entangled particles. Entangled particles are like genetic twins, such that a measurement of one can be considered a measurement on both. Therefore, according to EPR, you can make a precise position measurement of one particle and a precise momentum measurement of the other. That was an extremely clever idea. In particular, it identified entanglement as a property that could be used to test the predictions of quantum theory. The paradox is that while the Heisenberg uncertainty principle should be a fundamental property of quantum theory, entangled particles appear to violate it. This is a logical contradiction. However, there was one caveat. The EPR argument assumed that all properties of a particle were local to it (known as local realism). If quantum theory does not satisfy this principle of local realism, then the paradox is not valid. This property of local realism was later tested by John Bell in the form of an inequality: Any theory that satisfies the property of local realism will be bound by the inequality. All tests of Bell’s inequality have violated the inequality, indicating that local realism is not a fundamental property of nature.

Question: Is quantum mechanics an extension of statistical physics with more degrees of freedom and interactions among them? Does this explain why we obtain probabilities from calculations in QM?
Answer: Not really. Probabilities are obtained from QM calculations because we really don't know the mechanism (if any) that takes a non-local wavefunction to a localised detection. Rather, we use the Born rule to calculate a probability density from the wavefunction. You certainly can take the perspective that there is more under the hood than is represented by the plain vanilla theory. Indeed, Bohmian mechanics is one such interpretation that explicitly involves a statistical element. This is a hidden variables theory. QM was developed to describe empirical phenomena; notably interference phenomena. The interference required a wave theory, but localised detection was consistent with a particle theory. Glueing the two disparate aspects together required a statistical interpretation via the Born rule. This is essentially a top-down approach. In contrast, statistical mechanics relates macroscopic observables to microscopic dynamics involving many degrees of freedom, which requires statistical methods. This is essentially a bottom-up approach. As mentioned, of all interpretations, Bohmian mechanics is most closely related to a bottom-up approach, albeit with the addition of a guidance wave.

Question: What is the relationship between the concept of "randomness" in quantum mechanics and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle?
Answer: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle is a fundamental consequence of the structure of quantum theory. In particular, it can be viewed as a consequence of a wave theory, the consequence of a non-commutative algeba, or the consequence of a complex Hilbert space. All are equally valid, and point to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle as being indicative of the mathematical structure required to model reality. On the other hand, randomness is introduced via the measurement axioms. The measurement axioms act as a sort of interface to above-mentioned structure. That's primarily because quantum theory is formulated using complex numbers, while measurement results are given by real numbers. The measurement axioms (the Born rule and the collapse hypothesis) map a vector in a complex Hilbert space onto a real-valued measurement outcome using probabilities. So the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is ultimately a reflection of the underlying Hilbert space. It is really the fact that the Hilbert space must be mapped onto a measurement space that results in the so-called randomness of measurement outcomes.

Question: Is the wave function from a Schrödinger equation a physical representation of a location or simply a probability of finding something there?
Answer: I don't know what the wavefunction is. The best I can do is act like a detective and put together an identikit of the culprit. Is the wavefunction even necessary in a quantum theory? A colleague of mine who works in the foundations of quantum theory has stated that he'd like to see a quantum theory without the wavefunction. I can only suppose that's because actually understanding what the wavefunction represents can be quite challenging. The first thing to note is that the existence of a wavefunction is just an inference. The wavefunction cannot be directly detected. This is why we'll need some detective work to establish something about our culprit. The necessity for quantum theory stems from two properties that appear to be universal: All objects exhibit interference. Objects are detected locally. The first property can be explained by a wave theory. This is the origin of the wavefunction. Let's first consider a particle. A particle is represented by a point in space. That point can have attached properties, such as position and momentum. Note, this is just a representation of a particle. Particles are naturally detected locally. Now we have to consider the object to be associated with a wave in order to accomodate the interference phenomena. Furthermore, interference evolves, so the wavefunction must be associated with an equation that describes the evolution. This is the Schrödinger equation. In deducing that the object must be associated with a wave, we don't necessarily need to assume that the object and the wave are one and the same. For example, Bohmian mechanics treats the object as a particle and the wave exists to guide the particle. However, it is more common to consider the object to be represented by the wavefunction. When you do this you find that no single wavefunction will suffice. In particular, you need a specific function to represent the position of the object, and a different function to represent the momentum of the object. These are referred to as representations of the wavefunction. Thus the wavefunction is a representation of an object, and takes different forms depending on what you plan to measure. The relationship between the position and momentum representations of the wavefunction is given by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This effectively connects the two wavefunction representations to a single object. Note: the wavefunction is not a probability. In certain texts it is sometimes called a probability amplitude. The distinction is made because probabilities cannot interfere as they must be positive and the addition of two positive numbers cannot equal zero. However, the probability density can be obtained from the wavefunction by taking the modulus squared (known as the Born rule). So our wavefunction can be associated with a measurement probability. Its just that it also must allow for interference, which is associated with the object being distributed in space, rather than being localised. Ultimately, based on the two empirical properties that objects exhibit interference but are detected locally, we need a theory to accomodate both properties. This is the reason for the development of quantum theory. The fact that the two properties happen to represent contradictory concepts is the fundamental reason that its difficult to understand quantum theory. From a particle perspective, the wavefunction is better thought of as something related to a probability. However, from a wave perspective, the wavefunction is the object, but then localised detection becomes mysterious and not easily explained. This really is the reason that so many people adopt a shut-up and calculate approach.

Question: Recently a video was publish on YouTube claiming that NASA has developed (not tested) the ability to travel at light speed and a warp drive engine also known as the warp bubble. Do you think this is possible or true? If so what evidence either way?
Answer: Utter rubbish. There is amassing a body of theoretical work that is exploring a toy model constructed using Einstein's general theory of relativity. The ultimate arbiter for what is real is observation. We have never observed evidence for backwards travel in time, and the resultant contradictions lead us to think that it is simply not possible. This is led Stephen Hawking to propose the chronology protection conjecture. There is an ex-NASA employee who is a strong advocate for this technology, and other exotic new propulsion technologies. Question: Why aren't scientists more widely criticized for confirmation bias since they look for evidence to support their theory?
Answer: A few people are trotting out the old chestnut that the scientific method is based on falsifiability. Sure. You cannot prove that a theory is correct, but you can falsify it. However, scientists are human and certainly subject to confirmation bias. This has been born out spectacularly on a number of occasions, such as with the cold fusion debacle and the memory of water paper. I certainly have not embarked on a mission to falsify hypothises that I have had. Rather, I have worked to substantiate my hypothesis with empirical evidence. In essence, its a process of looking for the physical consequences of the hypothesis. If you can amass enough convincing evidence, then you might be able to get through peer review. This is a more natural way of working, and amongst the many colleagues I've worked with throughout the years, is probably the way most work. This is a process of working towards something. For a more high profile example, the Nobel prize awarded for the development of a Bose-Einstein condensate in dilute gases was a culmination of people working towards making this work. When they finally got their experiments to work, they had to substantiate their claims with experimental evidence. A similar process was recently evident with the LK-99 room temperature superconductor. In this case, the researchers didn't amass sufficient evidence for superconductivity. Their results were not reproducible, and the physical properties they reported were not deemed sufficiently convincing. Maybe these researchers were affected by confirmation bias. But in this case, it was reproducibility that was crucial in substantiating their claim, and they failed. These scientists have been heavily criticised by their peers, who are the only people sufficiently qualified to do so. In general, confirmation bias is usually picked up by your peers, either during peer review, or later. Most confirmation bias is minor, but if it is egregious, it can ruin a career. This is why scientists are generally scrupulously careful before announcing results. It is the process of convincing your peers that makes science generally self-correcting. That's usually what exposes confirmation bias.

Question: If we think of light as a bunch of photons, then how does it reflect from a surface? Almost all photons should have gone through the material's intermolecular space.
Answer: No no no… A photon is not a tiny billiard ball. In fact it has no uniquely defined size. A photon is a quantum of energy, and energy doesn't have a size. The electromagnetic field can be decomposed into various modes. An example of a field mode is a laser spot. If you have a good laser, such spots are a single mode. Now have some idea of the spatial extent of a mode. Not small at all. If there are no photons in the mode, it is called the vacuum state. You can add photons to the mode. This is just adding energy in discrete chunks. The photons are delocalized throughout the entire field mode. With this picture in mind, the photons interact with a large area of any reflecting body. As the field mode corresponds to an electromagnetic wave, the atoms in the reflecting body respond to the oscillating field, as they are charged particles. This response generates the reflected wave. Note, the reflected wave is caused by a coherent response, rather than absorption/re-emission. The coherent response can be envisioned as the atoms wobbling in phase with the incident wave. Any accelerating charge naturally generates an electromagnetic field. This is what is meant by a coherent response. In contrast, the absorption/re-emission process is not coherent. When there is a large area responding to the incident field, the reflected field can be expected to have similar mode properties. Overall, reflection is best treated in the classical picture, rather than the quantum picture. However, it is a requirement of the quantum and classical theories that one becomes the other in the appropriate limit. This is referred to as the correspondence principle.

Question: Why does Mach–Zehnder interferometer work? Won't the photon displace mirrors as it hits them? Final wavefunction will be superposition of photon from different paths also entangled with different positions of mirrors, then why would they interfere?
Answer: That's a nice question. You're asking why the entanglement rule doesn't apply to the Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The entanglement rule is simply put; entanglement destroys interference. I hate such blanket statements, which generally come from the mathematics describing a situation, rather than from some physical intuition. First, its instructive to look at the classical limit. The Mach-Zehnder interferometer works. It is a sensitive interferometer. That means that the effect of photon pressure on the mirror is negligible. In the theoretical description of a beam splitter, this is built into the model, which is represented by a simple 2x2 transfer matrix. That means we have to understand how such a simplification can be justified. The photon interaction with the mirror means that the mirror must be treated as a quantum object. However, the exact quantum state of the mirror is not well-known. That means it must be treated as a so-called classical mixed state. It is the mixed state of the mirror that needs to be distinguishable between reflection and transmission. Think of the mixed state as a probabilistic distribution of slightly different quantum states. Photon recoil will have a negligible effect on the various weights, such that the overall effect is that the mirror state can be considered to be a common factor (i.e., not entangled). If you were to do this rigorously, you would calculate the interaction using all the terms in the mixture, with the result being that the interfering terms dominate, while the other terms are negligible. A theoretician would say that the quantum state of the mirror contains no accessible which-path information.

Question: Why does quantum mechanics use complex numbers rather than real numbers?
Answer: This will be a non-technical answer that will hopefully be of benefit to a wider lay audience. The short and simple answer is that quantum theory is a wave theory. The reason for adopting a wave theory is because of the observation of interference effects. Interference is described using two properties; amplitude and phase. Complex numbers, consisting of a real and imaginary component, provide a natural representation of wave properties. Another reason is that complex numbers provide a very convenient way of representing rotations. That's because rotations are associated with a change in phase while maintaining a constant magnitude. With quantum systems, the total probability associated with the wavefunction must be unity. That essentially means the quantum system exists, which in turn means the evolution of the wavefunction corresponds to a rotation of some sort. Specifically, a rotation in Hilbert space. Rotations can't be represented using real numbers because real numbers only represent positions on a line. For rotations, we at least need a number system that describes a plane. EDIT: I have described the use of complex numbers as a convenience. However, there have been a few interesting comments about the property of complex numbers. One is the fact that the complex algebra is closed. That means that the roots of polynomial equations may not exist within the real numbers, but they do exist in the complex numbers. This extends to differential equations. As the evolution of the Schrödinger equation is described by a differential equation, you would expect that the existence of all solutions is an important property. It seems that the question of whether complex numbers are required for quantum theory has been debated for some time. I thank Don Holmgren in the comments for pointing out a recent paper in which the authors have derived an inequality that distinguishes been quantum theory based on real numbers from that based on complex numbers. Recent experiments are in agreement with the complex representation, thus raising the complex representation as a requirement rather than a necessity.

Question: How is Einstein's formula E=mc² related to Dirac's formula E=±MC²?
Answer: Let's start with the fact that the second formula is not Dirac's formula. The relativistic space-time invariant interval can be used to derive the formula, E 2 = m 2 0 c 4 + p 2 c 2 , which for a particle at rest ( p = 0 ) reduces to E = ± m 0 c 2 . The plus/minus ambiguity is simply dropped by convention considering energy to be positive. This is a classical equation for a massive particle. The Dirac equation was derived by quantizing the full mass-energy relationship to create a relativistic version of the Schrödinger equation. In order to do this, Dirac had to introduce a set of anti-commuting matrices that corresponded to a set of four equations, two of which corresponded to negative energy solutions. The fact that there were both positive energy and negative energy solutions corresponding to different equations meant that the negative energy equations could not be considered an ambiguity. This was ultimately interpreted by Dirac as the existence of a charge conjugate particle otherwise known as an anti-electron (or positron). The second equation of the question written using capital letters cannot be a shorthand notation for the Dirac equation because the two signs cannot be pulled out of the Dirac matrices (as depicted). They are integral to the structure of the matrices. Therefore the ± sign ambiguity is not an indication of the existence of antimatter as some of the other answers suggest. Moreover, the sign ambiguity associated with taking a square root is an example of a mathematical property that cannot be mapped onto a physical property. In the present context, that's because the existence of negative energy solutions would imply that the vacuum is not stable. Normally, energy loss is only possible for energies above the vacuum energy, which is the ground state. If negative energy solutions were possible, then there would be no ground state. Dirac actually grappled with this point and eventually proposed the Dirac sea concept, which was that all negative energy states were occupied, preventing further energy loss. However, modern interpretations of the Dirac equation do not use the Dirac sea. All energies are positive relative to a minimum energy ground state, and the signs in the Dirac matrices correpond to the CPT symmetry of the solutions. It is the CPT symmetry that is an indication of antiparticles.

Question: How do we reconcile the concept of underlying causes with the randomness observed in quantum physics?
Answer: Randomness is generally associated with lost information. With complex systems, the sheer amount of information present quickly becomes overwhelming. That's where statistical methods become useful. Behaviours are characterised by the statistics of repeated observation. The underlying dynamics are hidden. This means that randomness is an effective property, rather than a fundamental property. With quantum theory, randomness is often touted as being fundamental. That's because the full quantum theory is not a dynamical theory. Dynamical evolution extends only to the evolution of the wavefunction. This evolution is called unitary, corresponding to the rotation of a vector in Hilbert space. However, the full quantum theory is essentially a measurement theory. It is only concerned about predicting measurement results. The problem is that what constitutes a measurement is ill-defined. This introduces a non-physical element to the theory, which is referred to as the measurement problem. An alternative approach is to consider quantum theory to be an information theory. This sidesteps the issue of what constitutes reality. With an information theory, unitary evolution gives us the conservation of information. In this case, measurements act to select a subset of the available information, which means that there are multiple measurement possibilities. This brings us back to the use of statistical methods to understand a quantum system. If you have access to many copies of a quantum system, you can perform many different measurements to reconstruct the full quantum state. This is called quantum state tomography. Thus in both pictures, there exists an underlying quantum state that evolves deterministically. It is the act of measurement that gives a probabilistic result. Essentially, the measurement samples the quantum state resulting in information loss. This places quantum randomness as an effective phenomenon rather than a fundamental one.

Question: Is it scientific to claim that a paper is erroneous but be unable to identify any error within it which can be red-ringed?
Answer: Most physicists know of Noether's theorem; that a continuous symmetry is associated with a conservation law. This is one of the most powerful and useful advances in theoretical physics (its really mathematical physics). Space translation symmetry implies the conservation of momentum. Time translation symmetry implies the conservation of energy. Rotational symmetry implies the conservation of angular momentum. A beautiful theorem with wide ranging implications. So we have one theorem that gives us three conservation laws based on different symmetries. If one of the conservation laws were to be contradicted, then one of the symmetries must not hold. Space translation symmetry means that the laws of physics do not depend on position in space. Time translation symmetry means the laws of physics do not depend on position in time. Rotational symmetry means that the laws of physics have no orientation dependence. Let's suppose that we make an argument that angular momentum is not conserved. Noether's theorem then tells us that there must be a preferred orientation in space. That means all our physical quantities must be orientation dependent. So we would need to recast our theories in terms of x ( θ , ϕ ) and p ( θ , ϕ ) , etc., where θ and ϕ represent the orientation angles relative to some universal orientation direction. As this is not necessary to describe most physical phenomena, we can be quite sure that there is no preferred orientation in space and so angular momentum is generally conserved.

Question: When I learned Fourrier Transform that didn't give me a better intuitive understanding of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. If doing the math didn't give me the intuitive insight, what will?
Answer: I think that depends on exactly what you take away from learning the Fourier transform. I think that intuition is closely associated with familiarity. You can learn the mathematics of the Fourier transform, but that does not guarantee that you'll gain any insight. The same can be said about learning quantum mechanics. If you just learn the procedures for solving problems, you may not gain any real insight into the theory itself. I'm not sure that I can shed any more light on this subject, but I'll have a go. There are two common routes to obtaining the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship. One is via the Fourier transform, and the other is via the application of linear algebra. I personally find the second approach less intuitive, because it already assumes the mathematical structure of matrix mechanics. However, the derivation of the HUP is rather straightforward, based on the non-commuting property of matrices and the Cauchy-Schwartz inequality. This is the approach you use with discrete variables. On the other hand, the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is just a specific case of a general uncertainty principle that is readily apparent in the property of a function and its Fourier transform. For an intuitive approach, I prefer the Fourier transform. Now its important to understand the association of the Fourier transform with a physical system. In this case, the physical system is wave phenomena. Let's take a wave and model it using a mathematical function. In one dimension you can just use a sinusoid, such the f ( x ) = A sin ( k x ) . If we make the constant, A , a complex number, the phase ambiguity can be accomodated. Thus, f ( x ) is our mathematical representation of the physical wave. We can also represent a wave that varies in time, f ( x , t ) = A sin ( k x − ω t ) . Notice that we had to include another two variables, k and ω to give flexibility in describing an arbitrary sinusoidal wave. However, these variables are treated as constants that are chosen to specify the exact form of the wave. These constants can be determined by measuring how the wave changes with position and time. Therefore, if we were measuring position and time, we would choose f ( x , t ) to represent our wave. Let's suppose that rather than making position and time measurements, we are actually able to measure the other two variables. We previously referred to them as constants. That means if we were able to measure them directly, we would have all the information necessary to specify the wave. However, note that while our sinusoid exists over all points in space and time, it can also be equally well represented by just two constants. These constants are called conjugate variables. We could could equally well represent our wave using these conjugate variables using the function, F ( k , ω ) . This alternative k − ω representation of the physical wave is related to the x − t representation via the Fourier transform. What can we take away from this? The primary property is that a physical wave can have two different, but equivalent mathematical representations. The best representation to use really depends on what you are measuring. In the above example of an infinite sinusoid, the simplest representation would correspond to specifying the two constants (and the phase factor). There is no need to use an infinite amount of time or space to represent the sinusoid. Maybe you can see how this would be useful in areas like signal processing. The important point is that we can have different representations of a physical system. At least with waves. Now take a more general and realistic case where the wave represented by f ( x , t ) doesn't have infinite extent. Here the Fourier transform is not just two constants, but rather a function of finite extent in the variables, k and ω , F ( k , ω ) . Once more, both functions represent the same physical system, but in the more general case both functions have finite extent, but with the property that the product of the widths of the two functions is a constant. This is the general form of the uncertainty relationship. It is this constraint on the product of the widths that indicates that the two functions are representations of the same system. Now let's look at the two conjugate variables, k and ω . The former is called the wave-vector (it has a magnitude and direction) and is related to the wavelength by k = 2 π / λ , and ω is the angular frequency given by, ω = 2 π f . By moving to a more realistic representation with finite extent, we now have two conjugate representations; f ( x , t ) and F ( k , ω ) . The exent of one function has shrunk from infinity, while the other has broadened around the two constants. The extent to which one shrinks and the other broadens is precisely regulated by the uncertainty relationship. We now have four variables, but because two are conjugate to the others, they are associated with different functional representations of the same system. In optical imaging systems (such as microscopes and telescopes), these two functions are associated with different locations in the imaging system. The plane associated with the function f is called the focal plane, while the plane associated with the conjugate function F , is called the Fourier transform plane. The focal plane is where an image is formed, while the Fourier transform plane is often used for various types of image filters. While this can be done with physical systems, it is also possible to do digitally in programs such as Photoshop. Overall, this tells us that a physical wave has two conjugate representations. To move to quantum theory we use the de Broglie and Planck relationships, p = ℏ k and E = ℏ ω . The question is, what do these substitutions mean? How do we interpret them? The short answer is that they relate the momentum and energy of a particle to wave properties of wave-vector and angular frequency. Planck's constant essentially represents a coupling between wave and particle properties. The justification for moving to a quantum version of the Fourier transform is the observation of interference phenomena with so-called particles. Interference is treated using wave theory. In fact, the Fourier transform perfectly describes the observed double slit interference pattern. The properties of the Fourier transform means that position and momentum must be treated as conjugate variables. The general uncertainty relationship that is associated with the Fourier transform then becomes the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship. In essence, position and momentum have been decoupled, each associated with a different function. The function of position and the function of momentum are different, but related by the Fourier transform. For a quantum particle, the width of the position and momentum functions are coupled, satisfying the uncertainty relationship. As far as intuition is concerned, one has to understand the relationship between a function and its Fourier transform, and how two functions can be alternative descriptions of the same physical system. These functions refer to conjugate properties of waves. What does that actually mean? It means that one function describes the spatial properties, and the other function describes conjugate properties. The above pair of images illustrate the conjugate properties of an optical imaging system; the left showing the position representation and the right showing the spatial frequency representation. The physical system is the light used generate the two images. Each image is generated at different planes in an imaging system (focal plane left, Fourier transform plane right). Consider the left image as a position map, while the right image is a momentum map. Properties that can co-exist for particles do not co-exist for waves, in the sense that the momentum of a wave is described by one function and the position by another. When moving to the quantum Fourier transform, particles are now treated using a wave theory, and so position and momentum are described by different functions. Thus we have a physical system that is not described by a single function, but by two functions. These are referred to as the p- and x-representations. What is quite remarkable is that there two entirely independent approaches to deriving the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship. The quantum Fourier transform is suitable for continuous variables, while the spin properties are suitable for discrete variables. However, both approaches ultimately arrive at the same Heisenberg uncertainty relationship. This links Schrödinger's wave mechanics with Heisenberg's matrix mechanics, indicating that they were effectively the same theory. In fact, both the Fourier transform and the matrix mechanics formalisms are associated with a Hilbert space. However, a Hilbert space is an abstract mathematical concept, so probably not the best for developing an intuitive understanding of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Take 2: Let's attack this from a different direction. The Fourier transform approach directly give the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, and explains how it naturally arises when so-called particles exhibit wave-like properties such as interference. This is empirical fact. In other words, we observe this to be the case. Everything else follows from this observation. Therefore, it might be more instructive to ask what is Planck's constant? With respect to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, Planck's constant represents the minimum uncertainty associated with position and momentum variables. Consider the phase space representation of an object. Phase space is just a Euclidean plane that represents space ( x ) and momentum ( p ) on orthogonal axes. A classical particle at some time, t , can be represented by a single point in phase space. If we evolve that point over time, it traces out a curve. That unique curve associated with the particle dynamics is what defines determinism. Formally, the unique path corresponds to the minimum of a quantity called the action. If we add the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship, we can no longer represent an object with a point in phase space. Rather, the uncertainty defines a minimum area. Therefore, any dynamical motion will have an associated uncertainty that could accomodate many curves, which means the principle of least action cannot be applied. A phase space diagram that represents the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. This means that based on measurement outcomes, quantum theory is not deterministic. You many have read that Planck's constant represents a quantum of the action. This is a rather cryptic statement, but from the phase space representation we can understand it. What it means is that there is uncertainty in the action associated with an object. This is why Planck's constant has the units of action; it tells us that the action cannot be uniquely defined. Ultimately, the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship is derived from empirical phenomena such as the observation of interference. That means that the quantum description of such phenomena are not deterministic (in principle). However, quantum theory is a two part theory that includes a deterministic core (the Schrödinger equation) and some measurement axioms. The Heisenberg uncertainty principle pertains to measurements. This is why quantum theory can be considered either deterministic or non-deterministic, depending on your perspective. To understand this dichotomy, it might be instructive to look once more at the optical imaging analogy. The two planes are located at specific planes in the optical path, while the optical system evolves uniformly between the such planes. The smooth evolution of the optical signal corresponds to the deterministic Schrödinger-like evolution, while the imaging is limited by diffraction effects (akin to the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship). Hopefully, amongst all the above discussions, there might be something for your intuition to latch on to.

Question: Which one is the most common and holds more potential to produce qubits in quantum computers, photonic qubits or atoms ions electrons qubits? Why is that?
Answer: Each type of qubit has pros and cons. Photonic qubits have one big advantage, which is they are weakly interacting and well-isolated from thermal noise. That means decoherence is more manageable with photonic technology. The battle against decoherence is the reason why most quantum computers must operate close to absolute zero. In contrast, photonic quantum computers can operate at higher temperature (even room temperature). The company, PsiQuantum has recently secured multi-billion dollar funding. Its a bit of a dark horse because much of its technology is kept secret. However, I know the CEO from his post-doc days, and he's an extremely driven individual who has been developing this technology for about 20 years, and has a track record of delivering on his promises. The disadvantages are that photonic qubits must be generated deterministically for each run. This requires a large array of deterministic single photon sources, as well as high efficiency photodetectors. These are some of the technological issues of concern with photonic quantum computers. Other qubits have various advantages/disadvantages. The advantages are that the qubits exist and generally can be measured with high efficiency. However, many of these qubits are very sensitive to thermal noise. The ideal solid-state qubit would be insensitive to thermal noise. However, there are many other sources of environmental noise that can affect qubits in the solid-state. The superconducting qubits in particular are well suited to scaling up, being based on well-established lithography techniques. However, they are one of the most susceptible to thermal noise and manufacturing imperfections. These require cooling to close to absolute zero, and even then are still noisy. Colour centres in diamond are promising qubits, but cannot be easily fabricated in well-ordered arrays. They are promising because the qubit can be quite robust against noise. Furthermore, variations in the local environment means that optical techniques can be used to address individual qubits. However, optical addressing might ultimately limit scalability. This is a promising but immature technology. Single ions were one of the original proposals for a scalable quantum computer. However, it seems the plans for scalability were over estimated. The ions need to operate in a vacuum and require a sophisticated electrostatic trap configuration. This constraint seems to be one of the gotchas of this technology. Single atoms can exist either in an optical trap array in vacuum or as impurities in a solid-state system. Ultimately, arrays of atoms in an optical lattice might interface nicely with photonic systems, making some form of hybrid system. The solid-state atom approach has been vigorously pursued for decades, but has yet to yield a working computer with more than a couple of qubits. The potential benefit of this approach is extreme integration with electrically addressable qubits. This could deliver a solid-state version of a quantum computer with millions of qubits on a single chip. The bottom line is that a million qubit quantum computer seems to be more likely based on photonic qubits at this stage. However, whether this will ultimately be delivered remains to be seen. Roadblocks to any technological development are notoriously difficult to predict.

Question: What distinguishes quantum mechanics from classical mechanics? Why is quantum mechanics necessary when classical physics can solve many problems using Newton's laws?
Answer: In classical physics, particles act like particles, and waves act like waves, and never the twain shall meet. The classical physics of particles introduces point contact interactions and particle trajectories that follow unique paths. Newton's laws can be used to describe the dynamics of particle motion. Waves are described using a different theory. In particular, Huygens' principle describes the evolution of a wave, including diffraction phenomena and crucially, interference. In a material medium, wave mechanics can be reduced to particle interactions, leading one to suspect that the particle picture might be fundamental. When we add the concept of charges interacting with the electromagnetic field, particles then interact with the field, which mediates interactions with other particles. That's the next level of abstraction. The electromagnetic field, as described by Maxwell's equations, has wave solutions in the free field devoid of any charges. Here we have moved away from the particle picture completely. The mathematics of wave propagation is now appropriate. This really was the first stumbling block for classical physics. Wave propagation was assumed to require a medium. This gave rise the the aether theories, which were finally discarded with the development of relativity theory. In other words, the aether was not needed to support wave propagation. What was needed was a new perspective on space-time, known as Lorentz symmetry. That means that particles and waves were considered to be fundamentally different. This all changed when so-called fundamental particles were found to exhibit interference phenomena, which is a wave characteristic. This was a direct indication that what were considered to be particles actually exhibited wave-like properties. The degree to which particles act like waves was encapsulated in a new physical constant, called Planck's constant. This is why when you set Planck's constant to zero, you recover classical physics. However, Planck's constant, while small, is not zero. Therefore, one needs to adopt a wave-like picture for particles. In other words, you need to throw out your concept of what a particle is and adopt a new way of thinking. This is how quantum theory was born. This might still sound rather obscure and a bit silly, but the proof is in the pudding. The particles known as electrons are routinely used for their wave-like properties in electron microscopes. Electron microscopes represent a mature technology widely used around the world to image the finest details down to the atomic scale. The bottom line is that neither the particle nor wave pictures were adequate for describing all observed phenomena. What was needed was a conceptual readjustment that incorporated both pacticle and wave properties in a single entity from which particle and wave behaviours emerge in the appropriate limits.

Name: Mark John Fernee
Question: How can Schrodinger's equation, the many-worlds theory, and the Hamiltonian equations, one day allow one to quantum tunnel between different possible worlds?
Answer: So we're endeavouring to replicate Stargate here? There is only one quantum state… However, that quantum state cannot be described in three dimensional space. Rather, that state exists in an infinite dimensional Hilbert space. That's a nasty piece of jargon. I'm guessing that most people have never heard of the term. A Hilbert space is a mathematical definition that describes a class of functions and their properties. This a quite an abstract concept. However, it is also very powerful. You can derive quantum theory without reference to a Hilbert space. However, what you find is that the theory is naturally associated with this space. The quantum state comprises all possible measurement outcomes, while we measure only a single outcome. That's the origin of the many worlds interpretation. All the other possible measurement outcomes are considered different worlds. The question then is how can we state that there is only a single quantum state? This can be demonstrated with a quantum computer. Most quantum algorithms are deterministic. That means there is only a single answer. To get to this outcome, the quantum computer evolves the quantum state until it is properly aligned with what is being measured. This property is crucial for getting meaningful answers from a quantum algorithm. The deterministic output from a quantum computer tells us that there is indeed only a single quantum state. Mind you, if your quantum computer is not working properly, then the output will be probabilistic because the quantum state is not properly aligned with what is being measured. The question then is whether we can move from one world based on one measurement outcome, to another associated with a different outcome? There is no indication in the theory that this is even possible. The conundrum is that we only experience a single world, while inanimate objects like rocks exist across all worlds. Of course, rocks don't experience anything.

Question: If light is an electromagnetic wave, can you say that a candle flame is a source of electromagnetic waves? So if it emits electromagnetic waves, what is oscillating in a candle?
Answer: Actually, its rather complicated. A candle flame is a region above the candle. It glows yellow because it corresponds to an oxygen deficient region of the flame where complex carbon molecules form. These molecular agglomerates are commonly called soot. They comprise various carbon-based mollecular aggregates, including nanoparticles, such as buckminsterfullerene. When you have complex molecular composites, the excited state energy levels get smeared out. You no longer have discrete emission lines. What you have is thermal black-body emission. Thus the light is emitted by electrons in the carboniferous aggregates according to the local temperature of the hot gas. It is the wild thermal motion of these electrons that give the distinctive yellow/orange colour of a candle flame. If you put a metal plate into the yellow part of the flame, you can actually catch these soot nanoparticles before they are consumed by the flame. If you look at the soot particles under an electron microscope, you'll find all sorts of interesting molecules and carbon aggregates.

Question: Is Einstein’s “spooky action at a distance” a play on words with Newton’s “action at a distance”?
Answer: I believe so. Action at a distance is the idea that some action at point A can immediately affect spatially separated objects. For example, Newton's law of gravity embodies action at a distance, as it describes the forces experienced by two spatially separate masses, such that if you move one mass, the other would immediately experience a change in the force. Newton was aware of this implication of his law, but left it to others to resolve. This was done by Einstein in the development of his general theory of relativity. That means Einstein was instrumental in resolving the action-at-a-distance problem. Then along came quantum theory to rain on his parade. The Copenhagen interpretation of quantum theory had measurement-induced collapse of the wavefunction. As wavefunctions are generally non-local, the instantaneous collapse of the wavefunction would seem to imply some form of action at a distance. The tricky thing about the wavefunction is that it is not directly measurable. It is only inferred. So is something actually collapsing? The primary example of this phenomenon is entanglement. The measurement of one part of an entangled pair immediately constrains the possible measurement outcomes for the other, no matter their spatial separation. Is this action-at-a-distance? Well it has the whiff of it. However, entanglement collapse cannot be used to send signals. If it were bonafide action-at-a-distance, it could be used to send signals. That leaves us with something that seems like action-at-a-distance but that cannot be used as such. Spooky!

Name: Mark John Fernee
Question: Pls explain it to me, a mind not intelligent enough to understand. How can a photon be created, bounce around for millions years in the sun, break free and travel, and then die, all in the same instant?
Answer: It doesn't. If you are concerned about the last part of the sentence, then yes, it is completely nonsensical; and that is the clue that it is not the correct way to think about this. Anyone able to make observations… that means, anyone able to ponder space and time and the events that occur around us must always measure the same vacuum speed of light. That sets light apart from we observers. Light cannot observe. Light cannot have a perspective. Light just does what it does… move away from the source at the speed of light. So this statement about the sun is rather obtuse. In reality, it actually means that energy released in the core of the sun in a thermonuclear process takes a long time to diffuse outwards to the surface. This should be considered a thermal transport process. In no sense could you place some label on the released energy with its time of birth and track it for millions of years until it is detected as a photon here on Earth. Its just a statement that the core of the sun is much hotter than the surface because the heat released in the core cannot immediately escape. With heat flow, there are three processes to consider; conduction, convection, and radiation. The radiative process is the least effective of the three. The core of the sun is not transparent, so radiative heat loss would not be the primary mode of heat transport. That leaves conduction and convection. These processes are much slower. To properly understand the heat flow within the sun requires sophisticated numerical modelling. This is how the one hundred thousand year diffusion time is determined. Therefore, the idea that a photon is born deep inside the core of the sun and is somehow trapped there for millions of years cannot be substantiated. The photons we receive from the sun are emitted in the outer layer with an energy of around 2 eV. However, photons emitted by the fusion process are gamma rays with energies in the MeV range. That's millions of times more energetic. We should thank our lucky stars that these photons are not the ones bombarding the Earth. The proper way to think about it is that the energy released deep inside the sun takes around one hundred thousand years to reach the surface, where it heats the outer plasma layer to about 5000 K. It is the outer plasma that emits the light that makes its way to Earth. As observers, we note that it takes about six minutes for light to travel from the sun to the Earth. Different observers may measure different times, but then they will also measure a different distance travelled. However, all observers will agree that the light travelled with a speed calculated to be c. Finally, “the same instant” cannot be absolutely defined for spatially separated events. Rather we can map space-time with a grid of events. For light, the emission event and absorption event are different. Light moves uniformly from the emission event to the absorption event at the speed of light.

Question: Einstein believed quantum mechanics wasn’t fundamental and there must be a deeper theory. Was he correct?
Answer: Possibly. But it's also possible that we could never be able to develop such a theory. The key to the above statement is Bell's theorem; that no theory based on local realism can reproduce the results of quantum theory. Einstein's great insight into this problem was outlined in his famous EPR paper. Therein, he outlined measurements contrary to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle using entangled particles; coming to the conclusion that quantum theory must be incomplete. However, the EPR paper had assumed the property of local realism. Following the development of Bell's theorem, and associated Bell's inequality, experimental tests have sided with quantum theory, indicating that local realism is not a property of reality. So Einstein was wrong?! Not so fast. The EPR test is no longer considered a valid proof of incompleteness, as Bell's test results indicate that quantum theory is inherently non-local. While that has ruled out the entire class of local hidden variable theories, a deeper theory based on non-local hidden variable theories is still possible. The biggest outstanding problem with quantum theory, is that it is not strictly a physical theory. Rather it is a measurement theory. However, measurements are not well-described physically. This is known as the measurement problem, which was outlined with outstanding clarity by John Bell in an article titled, Against measurement[1] . The underlying principle physics is based on is the principle of determinism. In quantum theory, this is reflected in the principle of unitarity. That means the evolution of the quantum state is smooth, and consistent with causal interactions. However, this principle represents only half of the theory, which is the physical part of the theory. The entirety of the theory also includes measurement axioms, which are not physical. If the physical part of the theory provides a good description of reality, then it is possible that a deeper physical theory that solves the measurement problem might be possible. The physical part of the theory was put to the test in a 2019 paper that looked into the underlying physics of a quantum jump. Quantum jumps are a manifestation of the measurement problem, representing an irreversible change in a quantum state. Examples are radioactive decay, and more commonly the fluorescent emission of light, referred to as spontaneous emission. In the theory, these processes just occur unpredictably. The 2019 paper was notable for being able to detect the onset of a quantum jump and to reverse the process, thus illustrating that the jump itself was a purely physical process that occurred over a finite time. However, the authors note that the timing of the onset of the jump remains non-deterministic[2] . Getting back to Einstein. I suspect that Einstein, like many physicists, expected that the principle of determinism should hold. The non-deterministic element of quantum theory associated with measurement outcomes is contrary to this principle. Therefore it is logical to assume some deeper theory. Moreover, the fact that there is a metaphysical element to the description of the measurement process actually supports this contention. It may just be that the measurement problem is not solvable, because it describes what we observe, rather than the state of the system. This is a philosophical problem regarding the distinction between epistemic and ontic theories. Measurement theories are naturally epistemic, whereas physical theories are ontic. It may be that the ontic theory requires a god’s-eye-perspective. As such, it would be useless for predicting measurement outcomes. If Einstein were to be reincarnated, I'm sure he'd be fascinated with the modern understanding of quantum theory.

Name: Mark John Fernee
Question: Is the universe deterministic considering quantum probability?
Answer: I've discussed this before. Here I'll just give an example and a counter-example. The evolution of the quantum wavefunction is deterministic. This is called the principle of unitarity, and is put to use in the development of quantum computers. The prototypical random event is spontaneous emission. This punctuates deterministic evolution of an atomic system with a random quantum jump from the excited state to the ground state. The quantum jump has been shown to be a dynamical event in a recent experiment. However, to the best of my knowledge, there is no means for determining when the jump will occur. This is an inexplicably random element to the phenomenon. The principle of unitarity is considered to be fundamental. It effectively means that all effects have a definite cause. However, the unpredictable timing of spontaneous emission (and radioactive decay for that matter) seems to provide an example of a process with no discernable cause. The conflict of the unitarity concept with the timing of spontaneous emission is manifest in the many worlds interpretation of quantum theory. The many worlds theory has a problem with explaining what a measurement is. With spontaneous emission (and radioactive decay) there is a split into infinite worlds, each corresponding to every possible emission time. Thus determinism seems to require the existence of (infinitely) many worlds. However, these many worlds are really just a perspective. There is only one quantum wavefunction. The question is whether the wavefunction is real, or just a mathematical abstraction? Ultimately, deciding between whether nature is fundamentally deterministic or non-deterministic comes down to solving the measurement problem. In other words, the jury is still out on this question.

Name: Mark John Fernee
Question: How do we reconcile the concept of determinism with quantum indeterminacy in physics?
Answer: The Schrödinger equation is deterministic. It describes the evolution of the quantum wavefunction. This deterministic evolution forms the basis of how quantum computers work. Furthermore, quantum computers produce deterministic outputs. For example, Shor's factoring algorithm is deterministic. It would be useless as an algorithm if it were not so. The existence of such deterministic quantum algorithms is testament to the underlying determinism of the theory. The indeterminacy of quantum theory pertains to measurement outcomes. However, as already noted, not all measurements outcomes are random. Probabilistic measurement outcomes are indicative of a quantum state that is not aligned with the measurement axis. This results in projection onto the measurement axis that effectively determines the measurement probability. Ultimately it is this misalignment between the measurement and the quantum state that results in measurement indeterminacy. This indicates that a single measurement is generally insufficient for determining the quantum state. So while quantum state evolution is deterministic, measurements of the quantum state need not be. A quantum state is a representation of an object that is ultimately defined by measurement outcomes. Unfortunately, there is no unambiguous interpretation of the quantum state. If the quantum state is real, then a nondeterministic measurement outcomes represent a lack of information, rather than something fundamental. It would be nice if this was the last word on the matter, but with the collapse hypothesis, the measurement outcome becomes the new state. This is a manifestation of the measurement problem. The alternative to the collapse hypothesis is based on entanglement with the measurement apparatus. The information of entanglement is lost to the environment. Thus the collapse hypothesis is just an effective outcome based on information loss. This is compatible with the underlying determinism. Thus measurement indeterminacy is consistent with local sampling an underlying deterministic non-local quantum state. Alternatively, if we accept measurement outcomes as real, then the quantum state simply describes the different possible measurement outcomes. With this interpretation, the Schrödinger equation describes the evolution of the measurement probabilities, and indeterminacy can be viewed as fundamental. However, the case for the reality of the wavefunction rests in the observation of quantum interference phenomena. This was a primary motivation in the development of the theory. It is further supported by the fact that deterministic measurement outcomes are possible. The measurement-centric alternative is aligned with the epistemic approach, where no ontology is assumed. The bottom line is that the deterministic evolution of the wavefunction is generally viewed as being fundamental. This is referred to as the principle of unitarity. Measurement outcomes are generally non-deterministic, which can be attributed to information loss.

Question: If the idea of super-determinism in fundamental physics were true, how then would choices be made?
Answer: Superdeterminism is a very far fetched idea. In particular, it seems to only pertain to the violation of Bell's inequality. I'm not sure of any other consequence. Superdeterminism means that two seemingly random bit streams are not truly random. They contain hidden correlations that only become apparent in the violation of Bell's inequality. That means we have no independent statistical test that can reveal these correlations. In other words, there is nothing you can do to ensure that two bit streams are statistically independent. Mind you, people have gone to extreme lengths to obtain statistically independent bit streams (including the use of space-like separated sources), only to find that Bell's inequality is still violated. The alternative is that the bit streams are statistically independent and the violation reveals that the axiom of local realism is inconsistent with observation, as per Bell's theorem. As for making choices, this has more to do with determinism, rather than superdeterminism. However, most people do not clearly define what is meant by a choice. This enters the free will debate…

Question: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle says you can never know both position or momentum. Is that at that instant or even after the fact?
Answer: Think of it like this. A rotating sphere can have a north pole and a south pole. However, the two poles cannot be at the same point. They are by definition at the opposite ends of the sphere. More appropriately, a beam of light cannot be both focussed and collimated. They are mutually exclusive properties. A somewhat focussed beam can be said to be somewhat collimated, but the more collimated it is, the less focussed, and vice versa. This tradeoff in properties of a beam of light is described by an uncertainty relationship. This uncertainty relationship becomes the Heisenberg uncertainty principle in the quantum case. Then the diffraction limit becomes the Heisenberg limit. It might seem weird that an optics example maps directly onto the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In optics we are dealing with waves, whereas in the quantum case we are dealing with particles… or so most people think. However, the glue that joins these two disparate concepts is the observation of interference effects. What we conceive of as particles should not interfere, but interference is what is observed. Therefore our particles are not really particles, but something else. Rather, the particle description of matter is insufficient to describe all the phenomena observed with such matter. The observation of interference effects with matter is a good motivation for de Broglie's matter wave hypothesis, where the particle momentum is associated with a wavelength using Planck's constant, p = h / λ . It is the substitution of this relationship into the exponent of the Fourier transform that gives the Heisenberg uncertainty relationship. Going back to the light analogy. If we collimate the beam, it then remains collimated (within the constraints of diffraction). However, if you then focus the beam, it is no longer collimated. This is akin to making momentum and position measurements of a quantum particle. The physical system is the beam of light. The degrees of collimation and focussing are conjugate properties of the beam. Similarly, a particle is a quantum object that has the conjugate properties of momentum and position. It can take a while to grasp this, and some never do. When learning quantum theory, this is probably one of the most crucial aspects to take onboard.

Name: Mark John Fernee
Question: How can quantum entanglement have FTL speed across light years but be completely unable to transmit or transfer any information between particles?
Answer: The simple explanation is that both particles act as receivers. In an information channel there must be a sender and a receiver. With an entangled particle pair, both particles carry correlated information. Measuring a particle means that you are receiving that information. If both parties are receiving, then who is sending? So one party receives a random bit stream, and the other party also receives a random bit stream. There is fundamentally no method of imprinting meaningful information on a random bit stream. So what part of this is FTL? Two observers making measurements that each appear random? There are a number of phenomena that are FTL. In all cases, such phenomena do not transmit information.

Now we just have to wait and see.
